soul:
Sketch of a new theory of the human soul

Four or five gentlemen were debating, one night, several questions of high transcendence, without the disparity of votes bringing the slightest alteration to their spirits. The house was on Santa Teresa hill; the room was small, lit by candles, whose light mysteriously merged with the moonlight coming from outside.

But, if you want to hear me in silence, I can tell you a case from my life, in which the clearest demonstration on the matter under discussion stands out. First of all, there is not just one soul, there are two...

- Two?

- Nothing less than two souls. Every human creature carries two souls with him: one that looks from within outward, another that looks from without inward...

I am not referring to certain all-absorbing souls, such as the homeland, with which Camões said he died, and power, which was Caesar’s and Cromwell’s outer soul. These are energetic and exclusive souls; but there are others, though energetic, of changeable nature. There are gentlemen, for example, whose outer soul, in the first years, was a rattle or a hobbyhorse, and later a brotherhood stewardship, let us suppose.

For some days the two natures were balanced; but it was not long before the original one yielded to the other; there remained in me a minimal part of humanity. Then it happened that the outer soul, which before was the sun, the air, the field, the eyes of the young women, changed in nature, and became the courtesy and the flatteries of the house, everything that spoke to me of the rank, nothing that spoke to me of the man. The only part of the citizen that remained with me was that which had to do with the exercise of the commission; the other dispersed into the air and into the past.

I confess to you that from the very start I felt a great oppression, something like the effect of four walls of a prison suddenly raised around me. It was the outer soul that was shrinking; it was now limited to a few uncouth spirits. The ensign continued to dominate in me, although life was less intense, and consciousness more feeble.

Never were the days longer, never did the sun scorch the earth with more tiring obstinacy. The hours struck from century to century, in the old clock in the room, whose pendulum, tick-tack, tick-tack, struck my inner soul like a continuous flick of eternity. When, many years later, I read an American poem, I believe by Longfellow, and came upon this famous refrain:

Sleep gave me relief, not for the common reason of being the brother of death, but for another one. I think I can explain this phenomenon as follows: sleep, by eliminating the need for an outer soul, allowed the inner soul to act. In dreams, I dressed myself, proudly, in the midst of family and friends, who praised my bearing, who called me ensign; a friend of our house would come, and promise me the rank of lieutenant, another, that of captain or major; and all this made me live.

I put it on, made myself completely ready; and, as I was standing in front of the mirror, I raised my eyes, and... I tell you nothing; the glass then reproduced the full figure; not a line missing, not a different contour; it was I myself, the ensign, who finally found the outer soul. That soul, absent with the lady of the estate, dispersed and fled with the slaves, there it was, gathered back in the mirror.
house:
Sketch of a new theory of the human soul

Four or five gentlemen were debating, one night, several questions of high transcendence, without the disparity of votes bringing the slightest alteration to their spirits. The house was on Santa Teresa hill; the room was small, lit by candles, whose light mysteriously merged with the moonlight coming from outside. Between the city, with its commotions and adventures, and the sky, where the stars winked, through a clear and tranquil atmosphere, were our four or five investigators of metaphysical things, amicably solving the most arduous problems of the universe.

Here is how he began the narration:

- I was twenty-five years old, poor, and had just been appointed ensign in the National Guard. You cannot imagine what an event this was in our house. My mother was so proud!

You cannot imagine. If I tell you that Aunt Marcolina’s enthusiasm went so far as to have a large mirror placed in my room, a rich and magnificent work, which contrasted with the rest of the house, whose furnishings were modest and simple... It was a mirror given to her by her godmother, and that one had inherited it from her mother, who had bought it from one of the noblewomen who came in 1808 with the court of D. João VI.

All old, but good...

- Large mirror?

- Large. And it was, as I say, an enormous kindness, because the mirror was in the parlor; it was the best piece in the house. But there were no forces that could move her from her purpose; she replied that it was not needed, that it was only for a few weeks, and finally that “Mr. Ensign” deserved much more.

I believe that, if it had not been for the distress, she would have arranged the opposite; she would have left the brother-in-law and gone with me. But the fact is that I was left alone, with the few slaves in the house. I confess to you that from the very start I felt a great oppression, something like the effect of four walls of a prison suddenly raised around me.

Not from fear; I swear to you I was not afraid; I was a little bold, so much so that I felt nothing during the first hours. I was sad because of the harm done to Aunt Marcolina; I was also a little perplexed, not knowing whether I should go to her to give her the sad news, or remain in charge of the house. I adopted the second course, so as not to abandon the house, and because, if my sick cousin was badly off, I would only increase the mother’s pain, with no remedy whatsoever; finally, I expected that Uncle Peçanha’s brother would return that day or the next, since they had been gone for already thirty-six hours.

I think I can explain this phenomenon as follows: sleep, by eliminating the need for an outer soul, allowed the inner soul to act. In dreams, I dressed myself, proudly, in the midst of family and friends, who praised my bearing, who called me ensign; a friend of our house would come, and promise me the rank of lieutenant, another, that of captain or major; and all this made me live. But when I awoke, in broad daylight, the consciousness of my new and only self faded away with sleep — because the inner soul lost exclusive action, and remained dependent on the other, which stubbornly refused to return...

It is worth telling you that, since I had been left alone, I had not looked once at the mirror. It was not deliberate abstention, I had no reason; it was an unconscious impulse, a fear of finding myself one and two, at the same time, in that solitary house; and if such an explanation is true, nothing better proves the human contradiction, because at the end of eight days, I got the whim to look at the mirror precisely in order to find myself two. I looked and drew back.

I went back home, nervous, desperate, and threw myself on the parlor canapé. Tick-tack, tick-tack. I got up, walked about, drummed on the windowpanes, whistled.

At times I did gymnastics; at others I pinched my legs; but the effect was only a physical sensation of pain or tiredness, and nothing more. All silence, a vast, enormous, infinite silence, only underlined by the eternal tick-tack of the pendulum. Tick-tack, tick-tack...
